title: Do We Have to Teach History Chronologically
author: Lauren S. Brown
summary: Lauren Brown answers her title with a firm yes, and then adds that chronology and themes work together. She opens with a failed lesson in which she jumped ahead to Martin Luther King Jr.'s final years during a unit on the Great Depression and left students confused about when he spoke on economic rights. From that mistake she argues that chronology supplies cause and effect, the core cognitive work of history, and cites David Didau and Rikki Cole on sequencing and Sam Wineburg on students who cannot order events. She critiques the fact-and-year chart and offers a connected cause-and-effect organizer in its place. She then shows how recurring themes such as historical context shaping political choices, government of the people, and isolation versus intervention can loop back through a chronological spine and make knowledge stickier. Her closing rule is that novices need the chronological framework first, because a purely thematic approach works only for those who already have it.
points: Teaching events out of order, as with the King lesson inside the Depression unit, produces specific misconceptions because students cannot link effects to their causes.
Chronology is presented as the source of explanation in history, so a chart of laws and dates is weak unless students must show how each row leads to the next.
Recurring themes such as context shaping political choices let teachers loop back to earlier content, which strengthens memory and helps students spot patterns themselves.
The recommended structure is a strict chronological spine with thematic loops, since a purely thematic course suits only learners who already know the framework.
Brown flags periodization, meaning where units begin and end, as the next decision teachers should make visible to students.
quotes: In other words, chronology matters. It offers explanation. Cause and effect: one of the key tools used in history. That’s where the cognitive work begins.
Whether a student can correctly place the Korean War as 1950-1953 or World War II at 1939-1945 is less important than the chronology.
The real cognitive work is not knowing each of the items in a chart. It is in how each row connects to the one that follows.
Themes are what makes a great novel more than just a good story. They make the story more meaningful. The same is true in history.

Compromise is one especially important example of how historical context shapes political choices. Students, who are often idealistic, may want historic figures to be heroes and their choices to be clear-cut.
The chronology has to come first. A purely thematic approach works better for people who are already familiar with the chronological framework. Novices like our students need that framework first.
That’s how students begin to see history not just as a list of things that happened, but as a connected story in which the past keeps helping them make sense of what comes next.
